alignment.why: Both name a substantive concern raised in one committee and never raised in the other.
Both name a thin review resting on assertion, not scrutiny, that counted in that committee's decision.
Both name the same weakness or strength seen by both committees but given different weight.
Both name high scores from reviewers who could not or did not check the work, often at low confidence, counted at full weight.
Both name a higher tier that the committee's own record never argued for.
Both name a wrong, checkable factual claim about the paper that fed one committee's scores.
Both name an area chair setting the tier from their own reading, above what the reviewers supported.
Both name a rebuttal that moved one committee's scores and left the other's unchanged.
Both name a committee that knew of a substantive flaw, raised or admitted, and did not lower its scores.
Both name authors telling the two committees different things, so each judged different evidence.
Run 2 names an asymmetry in reviewers' knowledge of the baseline literature; run 1's R30 covers only a wrong novelty verdict and R05 only an unshared concern, neither the expertise mechanism.
Both name one committee refusing to credit promised revisions that the other committee accepted.
No run 1 reason names a headline claim judged overstated capping the tier; R05 is the broad unshared-concern reason, not this mechanism.
Both name an area chair adopting a single reviewer's position to settle the decision.
Both name one committee holding the same kind of contribution to an extra requirement, such as practical guidance from an analysis paper.
No run 1 reason names authors misreading or missing a reviewer's question.
Run 2 split from R18 the case where committees read the paper as different kinds of contribution; run 1's R36 keeps contribution-type standards together.
Both name similar verbal assessments placed at different points of the rating scale.
Both name a reviewer changing score after reading the other reviews, not the rebuttal.
Both name an engaged champion rating well above accept in one committee only.
Both name a meta-review misreporting its own reviewers' positions or concerns; R14 absorbed R25, which covers misreported final positions.
Both name scores rising on rebuttal clarifications or promises that nobody checked.
Both name an area chair's own judgement setting the tier against the reviewers' scores, here below them.
Both name a reviewer holding a below-threshold score after the rebuttal answered the main point, on secondary grounds.
Both name a reviewer's rating disagreeing with their own stated verdict.
Both name reviewers from another theoretical tradition contesting the paper's framing.
Both name an audience or venue-fit objection holding one committee's tier down.
Both name a low score held on a point peripheral to the contribution.
No run 1 reason names reviewers' distance from the field driving clarity verdicts; R32 concerns framing objections, not clarity.
Both name a discredited detractor that kept the area chair defending acceptance so a higher tier was never weighed.
Both name unsure reviewers settling on borderline scores that held the committee near the threshold.
No run 1 reason names an area chair deciding by a mean-score threshold against their own stated view.
Both name an area chair settling a split with an off-record reviewer's input.
Both name a reviewer's rating out of line with their own review text.
Run 1's R26 is reviewers not answering the rebuttal so scores stood; run 2's R26 is an area chair discarding such a score, a different mechanism.
Both name a review resting on less scrutiny (a partial reading) that still entered the decision.
Both name an area chair counting non-expert scores at full weight over checked assessments; here they held the tier down.
Both name an objection raised after the response period that the authors could not answer.

reasoning: Matched on mechanism, not wording. Run 2 split contribution-type standards (R16, R18) and peripheral held scores (R15, R20) that run 1 keeps together, and named silent score shifts (R22, R25) both under run 1's R08. Six run 2 reasons have no run 1 counterpart: literature-expertise asymmetry (R31), overstated headline claim (R39), authors misreading a reviewer (R11), field distance and clarity (R24), mean-threshold decision (R14), and the area chair discarding a silent detractor (R26). Run 1's R12, R20, R21, R28, R02, R26 and R30 have no run 2 match.
